doc.title: Dawoud Sabu Adeyola interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 30, 2025

title: Adapting to different leaders: Jamal, Turner, Allison, Dexter Gordon
summary: Listening, repertoire and reading; JAMAN's trio, Ahmad Jamal's use of space, Joe Turner, Mose Allison, and Dexter Gordon's One Flight Up.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Let me jump ahead a little bit. When I look at your list of people that you’ve collaborated with, you’re going everywhere from Big Joe Turner to Ahmad Jamal to Dexter Gordon and on. I’m trying to form a question about from a bass player standpoint do you feel you adjust your playing to the circumstance? I mean it almost sounds like oh of course yes, but people write about like Miles is quoted as saying that Ahmad Jamal taught him about using space. When you play with these variety of musicians how do you pick up on what you should be doing?

Well the first thing, like I tell my students in the university, the first thing you have to do as a bassist or a rhythm section player, I think it’s true you know, chord players — pianists, guitarists, drummers, but especially the bass player. You have to be a really, a good listener you know. But then you have to have a repertoire. I mean you have to know a lot of songs, a lot of tunes, a lot of patterns you know. I was fortunate when I first started playing around Buffalo there was a piano player named JAMAN. Jimmy Manuel. I was a part of his trio. And he had a — his repertoire book was like huge, you know what I mean? He passed on now. I should have done it but I’ve got a mind to ask — call his widow and ask what happened to that book he had, because he had a bunch of tunes in there. And so he would try to play all those tunes you know. And he had charts. So I learned a lot of standards and at that time the bossa nova was kind of getting big so he was on top of that. He had a lot of those, you know, songs from Carlos Jobim and whatnot. So that’s the first thing is to be familiar with the literature of music. And the second thing is you have to really listen because everybody’s different. As you mentioned, and Miles observed, Ahmad at the beginning he was known for using space, but when I got with him he was filling up those spaces more. You know and he was playing like really — and so he was really — some of the critics said that they attributed — that maybe I had a little influence on him because I was kind of a heavier, you know, I had like a heavier touch. But if you listen to those, like what we did in France with Gary Burton is really the way he played “Manha de Carnaval” and all those — it was really hot and it was really a lot. And with Peyton Crossley on drums who — you know Peyton Crossley and Tony Williams had the same teacher in Boston, Alan Dawson. And Roy Haynes is from Boston too. So there’s a certain thing about those Boston drummers that they brought with them to New York. But yeah, no, that’s a long answer but basically you have to be a really good listener because everybody plays differently. For instance when I played with Joe Turner, if I remember correctly, he’s known as a blues player, right? He did blues all night and everything was in the key of C. You know? Everything. But — and he brought his own piano player. But it didn’t sound like it, it was all different

you know. Same thing with Mose. On the other hand Mose Allison was known as a blues guy but he played very little traditional — I mean it always had the blues feeling, a heavy blues feeling, which really was remarkable, you know, especially for a white musician. I think he’s from Mississippi or somewhere like that. But he had this real nice, and he was an excellent pianist too actually. All of his music, it had chord changes. It had charts. When you listened to it, it sounded oh yeah he’s playing his blues, but there were always different chord changes in it. You know? So that’s the third thing. The first thing is you’ve got to know a lot, you know you have to be familiar with the literature and you have to be able to listen. Then you also have to be able to read music because a lot of times these guys they come in and there’s not — very little rehearsal. Like with Dexter we had one rehearsal. And at that time he had done that recording with Donald Byrd and what’s her name, it was a Donald Byrd composition — I can’t think of the name of it. But anyway it’s a little different. The form was really different you know. And so he said, “Yeah, you know sometimes people ask for this so we tried it a little bit.” At that time Virgil Day was the drummer and John Weiss was the piano player. And we looked at it a little bit and just said, “Ah na, it’s too hard, we won’t do it.” So in the middle of the set, we were at the Tralf downstairs, that you mentioned. In the middle of the set, Donald Byrd had been playing in town. I think he did a concert at one of the universities for Buff State. So he walks into the club. He heard Dexter was there so he walks into the club. So people see him and they immediately start requesting this song that we decided we weren’t going to do. And Dexter says — he had this deep voice — “Hey people, they want us to play Donald’s tune you know, what do you think?” And I said “Well you know, we’ll follow you man.” So it came out all right. “One Flight Up.”
Do you remember that one? Yeah. It’s got a strange form to it you know. It’s a long form to it too.
